text: Last lesson covered why location-based trust broke down. This lesson covers what NIST SP 800-207 proposes instead: seven specific tenets that define a Zero Trust Architecture. These aren't marketing language, and they aren't a product checklist — they're architectural requirements straight out of Section 2.1 of the actual publication, and you're going to map every one of them to controls you already know.

The first three tenets set the scope. Tenet one: every data source and computing service counts as a resource — SaaS apps, APIs, containers, IoT, not just servers. Tenet two: communication is secured the same way regardless of network location, so being on the internal network earns a connection nothing extra. Tenet three: access is granted per-session, not carried forward — the real reason behind short-lived OAuth tokens instead of all-day VPN sessions.

The next four tenets govern the decision itself. Tenet four is the big one: access is determined by dynamic policy — identity, device state, and context evaluated together, every single time, which is exactly what a Conditional Access policy already does. Tenet five keeps monitoring device posture continuously, never on a one-time pass. Tenet six enforces authentication and authorization strictly before access, every time. And tenet seven feeds all of that telemetry back in to keep improving the policy itself.

Notice what's absent: no tenet tells you to deploy a specific gateway or buy a specific product. These are requirements an architecture has to satisfy, assembled from whatever you already run — Conditional Access for dynamic policy, Intune or Systems Manager for continuous posture, OAuth tokens for per-session access, SIEM and XDR pipelines closing the feedback loop. You already own most of the pieces.

What's still missing is the part that actually makes these decisions in real time and applies them at the point of access. Next lesson names those components directly: the Policy Engine, the Policy Administrator, and the Policy Enforcement Point — the three logical pieces NIST's own reference architecture uses to turn these seven tenets into an access decision that actually happens.
